searchText: Hi Micah. Looking at the ``ethereum-crypto/library/source/secp256k1.ts`` code, I noticed that you choose to sometimes reverse ``s`` and consequently ``R.y`` in the ``sign`` function. The comment is: ``// if there are multiple valid values of s, prefer the smaller one`` ``const s = maybeS < basePointOrder / 2n ? maybeS : basePointOrder - maybeS`` [...] Could you please explain that choice to me? Is this formally specified somewhere? Or is it just to speedup the double&add algo? IIRC (it was a while ago) this is an Ethereum thing to avoid needing 4 values for `v`? Though, I may be thinking about something else. Hmm, actually maybe that is the `if (point.x >= basePointOrder)` thing that I am thinking of. <@273808422753796097> probably remembers why `s` is changed if it ends up being greater than half of the base point order. It's to make signatures not malleable So to prevent third parties from changing the signature while the tx is inflight Meaning, two valid signatures for a single transaction? Yep Where third parties can flip which one it is Which could cause the included txhash to be different from the sent txhash Which would screw up ux Oh, you don't need the private key to flip between the two? No you don't Yeah, I see it now. Thanks! With the private key, you can make almost 2**256 different valid signatures for each (tx, key) pair BLS is the only scheme we have (well technically lamport/winternitz too) which tries to have a "one valid signature per (message, key) combo" property That is a neat property. Are there any big wins from it, or just "simplifies some things"? So should a node/wallet assume that signatures with ``s > PointOrder/2`` are invalid? Since a specific bloc? Nevermind, I think I found the specification. It appeared in the EIP-2 for the Homestead hardfork (a while ago!) Thank you both for your kind help! 🙂

Hi Micah. Looking at the ``ethereum-crypto/library/source/secp256k1.ts`` code, I noticed that you choose to sometimes reverse ``s`` and consequently ``R.y``  in the ``sign`` function. The comment is: 
``// if there are multiple valid values of s, prefer the smaller one``
``const s = maybeS < basePointOrder / 2n ? maybeS : basePointOrder - maybeS`` [...]
Could you please explain that choice to me? Is this formally specified somewhere?

excerpts.author: arxis75
excerpts.content: Or is it just to speedup the double&add algo?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: IIRC (it was a while ago) this is an Ethereum thing to avoid needing 4 values for `v`?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Though, I may be thinking about something else.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Hmm, actually maybe that is the `if (point.x >= basePointOrder)` thing that I am thinking of.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: <@273808422753796097> probably remembers why `s` is changed if it ends up being greater than half of the base point order.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: It's to make signatures not malleable

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: So to prevent third parties from changing the signature while the tx is inflight

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Meaning, two valid signatures for a single transaction?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Yep

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Where third parties can flip which one it is

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Which could cause the included txhash to be different from the sent txhash

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Which would screw up ux

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Oh, you don't need the private key to flip between the two?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: No you don't

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Yeah, I see it now.  Thanks!

excerpts.content: That is a neat property.  Are there any big wins from it, or just "simplifies some things"?
